task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-02, in the area of lineup and matchup effects):
Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: shot mix (rim, midrange, three-point shares; shot distance)
lineup fixed effects and placebo contrasts
methodological_questions: Does a one-player change in the offensive five shift team shot mix by the amount the player swap predicts?
Is the positive control informative, or is it near-tautological because the shooters change?
How should opponent, score state, clock and period confounds be separated from personnel effects?
Is there enough exposure per unit, and how should sparsity and multiplicity be handled?
Do placebo or null contrasts separate a real personnel effect from construction artifacts?

historical_evidence.finding: A PULL_UP exposure-effect study found the effect shrank from -0.0255 with lineup FE to -0.0063 without lineup FE. The same-shooter placebo on other play types was -0.0075. [prior work] attributes this to a shooter-level confound (C_artifact, limited by confounding, risks CONFOUNDING and PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE).

An audit of a published suppression excess reproduced 0.4080 but found it indistinguishable from a within-unit permutation null (residual +0.0054, z 0.40). [prior work] cites drift, insufficient exposure, regression to the mean and a mechanical floor as limits.

A double-suppression stacking study had a large baseline (n=960,764) but a small stacked cell (n=1,047). The stacked delta was -0.071 against an additive prediction of -0.232. [prior work] lists limits of implementation bug and small sample.

A penalty-state pilot (3->4 team fouls) was not distinct from its placebo contrasts. Standard errors were not printed because of a sqrt warning. [prior work] gives the mechanism as unclear and the risk as PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE. Its method used game x offense x period FE with 2->3 and 4->5+ placebos.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Attributing an exposure effect to defensive adaptation without controlling for shooter/lineup composition.
failed_approaches.why: The effect depended on lineup FE, and the same-shooter placebo showed a similar slope, consistent with a shooter-level confound (artifact, confounding).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Reading a trigger-versus-matched-control excess as a real effect.
failed_approaches.why: The excess matched within-unit permutation nulls, with drift, sparse exposure, regression to the mean and a mechanical floor (artifact).

failed_approaches.what_failed: A pilot contrast that was not separable from its placebos, with unprinted SEs.
failed_approaches.why: Placebo contrasts were as large as the target contrast, and the mechanism was unclear (inconclusive).

evidence_establishes: Earlier project work shows that lineup/shooter composition is a major confound in play-level effects ([prior work][prior work], recorded as artifact).

Placebo and null-model contrasts, and permutation nulls, are needed to separate real effects from construction artifacts ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]).
Sparse cells and unprinted or invalid SEs have previously left results inconclusive (FAM:[prior work], [prior work][prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: No retrieved record tests whether changing the offensive five shifts shot mix, so this question is not answered by prior work.
Nothing retrieved gives the size of a shot-mix shift per player swap, or the power available for it.
[prior work] do not show whether the project's lineup-FE designs can detect a known personnel effect. That is the very point of this positive control.
own_inferences: That personnel changes shift shot mix is close to mechanical, because different players take different shots. Detecting a shift is therefore a weak positive control. A stronger one tests whether the size of the shift is predicted by out-of-sample player shot profiles.

Because the retrieved failures are artifacts from composition confounds, the control must predict a graded, signed, magnitude-specific shift, with null swaps (similar-profile players) predicting no shift.
Pooled single-swap events should give ample power. Individual five-man units will be too sparse for unit-level inference.
Substitutions are non-random, since coaches substitute by score, fouls, fatigue and matchup. Pre/post comparisons may therefore carry selection and context confounds.
uncertainties: Retrieval returned only indirectly related records. A direct prior study of lineup shot mix may exist but was not returned.
Shot-profile reliability per player (FGA counts per player-season) is unknown here.
The effect size per swap and the number of clean single-player substitution events are unknown without running the data counts.
Play-by-play shot-distance and zone coding may have drift across seasons.

historical_effect.explanation: Without [prior work] I might have simply proceeded with a lineup-change versus shot-mix comparison. The retrieved artifact and placebo-dependence findings moved the decision to proceed_with_changes. The changes are: a dose-response test against held-out player profiles, explicit null swaps, within-game matching, permutation nulls, and pre-specified handling of exposure and SEs.
